hints: Compare what is attached to the $\text{COO}$ group in each acid, $\text{CCl}_{3}$ versus $\text{CH}_{3}$, and think about how chlorine affects electron density compared with hydrogen.
walkthrough:
Picture what acidity really means**
Think of the acid dissociating: $\text{RCOOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{RCOO}^{-} + \text{H}^{+}$. A stronger acid is one where this equilibrium lies further to the right. That happens when the anion left behind, the carboxylate ion, is more stable.

See how chlorine helps the anion**
Chlorine is very electronegative. Three Cl atoms pull electron density towards themselves through the sigma bonds, the -I effect. This spreads out and delocalises the negative charge on $\text{CCl}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$, stabilising it. It also pulls electrons away from the $\text{O-H}$ bond, weakening it. So the proton is lost much more easily than from $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$.

Final answer: The three Cl atoms exert a strong electron withdrawing -I effect which stabilises the $\text{CCl}_{3}\text{COO}^{-}$ anion / weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond, so $\text{CCl}_{3}\text{COOH}$ loses $\text{H}^{+}$ more readily.

hints: Recall the general change $\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{COCl} + \text{SO}_{2} + \text{HCl}$ and notice ethanedioic acid has two $\text{COOH}$ groups to convert.
walkthrough:
Apply the standard SOCl2 recipe twice**
You know $\text{RCOOH}$ becomes $\text{RCOCl}$, with $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$ formed. Here the starting acid is $\text{(COOH)}_{2}$, which is $\text{HOOC-COOH}$, so it has two $\text{-OH}$ groups to replace by two $\text{-Cl}$ atoms. That means you need two molecules of $\text{SOCl}_{2}$ and you make two molecules each of $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$ to balance Cl, S, O and H.

hints: Think what warm acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ does to a $\text{COCl}$ group after hydrolysis, ethanedioic acid is easily oxidised to a familiar gas.

For the diamine, count atoms in $\text{(COCl)}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{NCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ and use the formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{6}\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{2}$ to see that two $\text{HCl}$ molecules are lost and both ends join to give a cyclic diamide.
walkthrough:
Spot the oxidation product**
$\text{(COCl)}_{2}$ hydrolyses very readily and the ethanedioate part is already highly oxidised. Warm acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ cleaves the central $\text{C-C}$ bond completely. Each carbon ends up as carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_{2}$, which is the only carbon containing product.

Build the ring with the diamine**
An acyl chloride plus an amine gives an amide plus $\text{HCl}$. Here you have a diacyl chloride and a diamine. One $\text{-COCl}$ reacts with one $\text{-NH}_{2}$ at each end, losing $2\text{HCl}$ in total. Because both molecules are short and bifunctional, the two ends join together to close a six membered ring: $\text{O=C-C=O}$ on one side and $\text{HN-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-NH}$ on the other. Check the formula: that ring is $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{6}\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{2}$, exactly as given.

Final answer: With warm acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}(\text{aq})$: $\text{CO}_{2}$
With $\text{H}_{2}\text{NCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$: cyclic diamide, a six membered ring $\text{-CO-CO-NH-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-NH-}$ closed head to tail, with two $\text{C=O}$ amide groups.

hints: Recall that $\text{COCl} + \text{OH}$ gives an ester link $\text{COO}$ plus $\text{HCl}$, so join $\text{-CO-CO-}$ from the diacyl chloride to $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-}$ from the diol.
Remember to show two complete repeats with all $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O}$ bonds displayed and continuation bonds at the ends.
walkthrough:
Link the monomers by ester formation**
Each $\text{-COCl}$ reacts with an $\text{-OH}$ to make $\text{-COO-}$ plus $\text{HCl}$. So the $\text{(COCl)}_{2}$ unit contributes $\text{-CO-CO-}$ and ethane-1,2-diol contributes $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-}$. Put them alternately.

Extend to two repeats**
Draw $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-C(=O)-C(=O)-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-C(=O)-C(=O)-}$ with free bonds continuing left and right. Keep every $\text{C=O}$ shown fully, because the question asks for functional groups to be displayed. That is two full $\text{[O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-CO-CO]}$ repeats joined together.

Final answer: Two repeat units: $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-CO-CO-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-CO-CO-}$ with all ester $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ groups displayed, continuation bonds at each end.

hints: Recall which functional group gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}(\text{aq})$ and what that solid is called.
walkthrough:
Recognise the classic test**
A yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$ is the positive iodoform test. It tells you H contains a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ group or a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)-}$ group that can be oxidised to it. The yellow solid itself is always triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_{3}$.

hints: Read the peak heights in Fig. 9.2 as relative numbers of protons and use Table 9.1 to assign each chemical shift to a proton environment.
Apply the n+1 rule in reverse: a singlet means zero protons on adjacent carbons, a triplet means two, a quartet means three.
Match $\delta$ 1.15 and 3.95 as a coupled $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-CH}_{2}$ pair, and $\delta$ 2.25 and 3.60 as isolated singlets.
Check the total adds to 10 H for $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$ and fill all twelve boxes systematically.
walkthrough:
Use shift to find the environment**
$\delta$ 1.15 is alkane $\text{-CH}_{3}$, $\delta$ 2.25 is alkyl next to $\text{C=O}$ ($\text{CH}_{3}\text{-C=O}$), $\delta$ 3.60 and 3.95 are alkyl next to electronegative O ($\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-}$). That already points to an ethyl ether plus a methyl ketone fragment.

Use splitting to count neighbours**
Singlet means n = 0 neighbours. Triplet means n = 2 neighbours (3 peaks = 2+1). Quartet means n = 3 neighbours (4 peaks = 3+1). So $\delta$ 2.25 singlet and $\delta$ 3.60 singlet both have 0 protons on adjacent carbons, $\delta$ 1.15 triplet has 2, $\delta$ 3.95 quartet has 3.

Use integration for numbers of protons**
Peak areas give 3H, 3H, 2H, 2H respectively, total 10H matching $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$. The 3H triplet at 1.15 coupled to the 2H quartet at 3.95 is the classic $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-}$ ethyl pattern. The 3H singlet at 2.25 is isolated $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C=O}$, and the 2H singlet at 3.60 is isolated $\text{-CH}_{2}-$ with no H on neighbours.

Final answer: $\delta$ 1.15: triplet, 3 $^{1}$H, 2 adjacent protons; $\delta$ 2.25: singlet, 3 $^{1}$H, 0 adjacent protons; $\delta$ 3.60: singlet, 2 $^{1}$H, 0 adjacent protons; $\delta$ 3.95: quartet, 2 $^{1}$H, 3 adjacent protons.

hints: Combine the clues: no reaction with $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ rules out acid, iodoform test requires $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$, and NMR requires $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{O-}$ plus isolated $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ and $\text{-CH}_{2}-$ fragments.
walkthrough:
Assemble the fragments into H**
H is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$, gives iodoform so it has $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$, seen as the 3H singlet at $\delta$ 2.25. It does not fizz with $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ so it is not a carboxylic acid, but it has three O atoms, so think ketone plus ester. NMR shows $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{O-}$ (1.15 triplet + 3.95 quartet) and an isolated $\text{CH}_{2}$ singlet at 3.60. Joining $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ to $\text{-CH}_{2}-$ to $\text{-COO-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{COOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, which fits all shifts, splittings and the formula.
